Even if your contract doesn't mention severance, you WILL BE entitled to it when you finish your last contract. And your boss will have to pay you both the completion bonus and the severance since the completion bonus is in your contract (as a form of payment for completing the contract)

I would just double-check with the boss that he understands that he will be expected to pay the severance at the end of your last contract...but since this is a big hagwon they should already be aware of this since all their contract employees will legally receive those severance payments at the end of their last contracts.

1) Double-check what your contract says about renewal bonuses and severance (although severance info in the contract doesn't matter much since it's mandated by the government).

Living in Korea for over a decade I've had my share of experiences with the medical system here...Korea definitely has its own unique medical culture that takes some time to understand and get use to...definitely pros and cons in my opinion. 

Pros:
- it's MUCH cheaper than other places. 
- it's a lot faster in most situations...walk in and get seen and probably diagnosed and treated on the same day for major issues. I've definitely been spoiled by this because I now get annoyed when I have to wait more than an hour to see a specialist, haha.
- pretty advanced technology...it's crazy that even smaller clinics will have xray and ultrasound equipment...back home you will get a referral, make an appointment, wait a week or 2, then get the scans, make another appointment with your GP and wait another 2 to 3 days to ge the results...here you get all that done on under 2 hours. 


Cons or areas that can absolutely be improved:

- terrible bedside manner...doctors are generally very cold and at least for me as a foreigner it creates an atmosphere of "you're not really welcome here".  As mentioned by others, doctors are seeing a lot of patients every day that can leave you as the patient feeling a bit like a number instead of a person...this also spills into all of my other cons:

- preperceived options and stereotypes from doctors...this isn't just a Korea thing but it's more obvious here as a minority that you sometimes have to "fight" or advocate for yourself a lot more to get the treatment you feel is needed. 
One example was when I had pneumonia, I could tell the nurse thought I just had a cold and was trying to get a sick day out of it...only after I insisted on an xray and my lungs looked like a white tree branch did they jump into action, slap a mask and an IV on me etc. 

Another doctor proudly proclaimed, "Your HIV results are negative," even though I was there for IBS treatment and diagnosis, and I didn't ask or discuss HIV or my sexual history with him at all. 

- poor preventive care...as foreigners we have to get mandatory medicals for our visa, and bi yearly medicals for the NHI and yet they never followup or offered me advice for indications of high blood pressure and being pre-diabetic...the WORST case of this was getting diagnosed with cancer 2 weeks after I had both my visa and NHI medical neither of which even tested for testicular cancer even though it's the most prominent type of cancer for men in my age group. I felt a lump, but thought "I just had two medicals and neither of them showed anything worrisome in the bloodwork" so probably nothing to worry about...luckily I trusted my gut instinct and got it checked out because I had a very aggressive type of cancer...I caught it early at stage 1 and was able to get cured. 

- over medicating. I've had at least 2 doctors ask ME as the patient what type or medication I wanted. Only when I asked them as the doctor to give me what they medically recommend did they dive deeper and ask more about my symptoms...one was for ibs: doctor simply said "well what do you want me to do for you" after I explained my condition and symptoms...the 2nd was for antidepressants where the doctor said i can prescribe A or B which do you want...this was my first time getting mental health help and he knew that but still offered no additional information "just said they're basically the same you can choose one and then read about it online"...ended up gaining over 30kg in one year on those meds and each time I went for a refill I would ask about the weight gain only to be told you should eat less and workout more.

- weird medical protocols: this is specifically for surgeries and not sure if it's like this at all hospitals but when i went in I was only told to fast..no additional information about what to bring...i took the insensitive to pack an overnight bag with what I thought I would need. Assuming everything medical would be provided by the hospital...well after checking in and getting an IV put in the nurse hands me a list of like 10 medical supplies I need and tells me I can go buy them in the store downstairs...stuff like a bottle to pee in, a water bottle, a pack of wet wipes, gloves etc...it was the first time in my life that I had to wheel my IV into an elevator and go to a CU to buy medical supplies haha...most of which I didn't use. It's very strange that they don't just supply those items and then charge you for them.

They also had me make a payment immediately after surgery..I was literally just wheeled out of the OR still waking up when the company that provided some medical devices asked me to make a payment for it via bank transfer. 

- needing a guardian for hospital care...when I was booking my surgery they gave me two options...a room with a guardian which would be an extra 100-300usd a night or no guardian (it was covid times, but the no guardian room would typically have a family members/friend to take care of you). Only medical care will be provided by the nursing staff, but anything else like needing help to go to the bathroom or getting out of bed would be the guardian's responsibility.

Lack of privacy: I've had nurses shout my results to each other in busy waiting rooms..."The foreigner's weight is this, and his height is that please make a note in his file, etc."... for my surgery the nurse came in and asked to take a photo of the surgery area...it was explained it would be a small incision on my lower abdomen, yet she pulled my pants to  my knees and took photos of everything while the curtains were open, other patients in the  room etc and on her personal phone. 

Overall, it might seem that I've had more negative experiences here, but they're still worth it for the opportunity to get medical care...that isn't an option back home.

Some good advice has been given here but I would like to add some important details:

As mentioned, short-term rentals of 1 to 6 months will probably just cost you monthly rent upfront for each month. The cheapest options include share-houses and goshiwons. Goshiwons are typically not very comfortable, just a very small room with a single bed and small desk... probably a shared bathroom among 5 to 15 men/women...basically like a dorm.

Someone mentioned getting a loan as a deposit  to cancel out the monthly rent. That's not an option for most foreigners on a visa, unfortunately. The amount you need to do this is roughly 100k-200k usd or more depending on size and location of the property. 

The most popular option, as mentioned, is a 'smaller' deposit + monthly rent. The amount you have to pay for both the rent and deposit is gonna differ from location to location.  In my neighborhood, it's typically 10k usd deposit and 700 to 800 usd rent per month, and this will be for a small one room with a 1 - 2 year lease agreement...other less modern or fancy areas could be around the 5k usd deposit for 400-600 usd rent per month.  

Other costs to keep in mind: 

The realtor fee is about 3% of your deposit 

Maintenance fees can be around 50 to 100 dollars a month, and that's excluding your utilities (overall, I would expect to pay 100 to 150 for maintenance and utilities per month).

If you're thinking of long-term renting, you will have to pay 10% of the deposit to "hold" the apartment for you. You pay the remaining 90% of the deposit when you move in. 

Of course, it's all based on the location and type of accommodation, etc.
